d.title: Five blocking habits, and the await that replaces each
d.caption: **One synchronous `requests.get` taking two seconds does not delay your conversation by two seconds — it freezes the whole event loop, so every other conversation in the process stops too**, including ones nowhere near that tool. The symptom is latency that worsens with traffic in a way no single trace explains, and the cause is invisible in the trace of the request that suffered. **Audit tools for synchronous IO the way you audit them for credentials.**

steps.code: the cost of getting it wrong

d.title: The rule is not 'always async' - it is 'anything that waits must await'
d.caption: **ADK accepts an ordinary `def` tool, and for anything that does not wait that is the better code:** arithmetic, formatting, a dictionary lookup, a quick validation. A synchronous function that never does IO is simpler to read and costs nothing. **A synchronous function that opens a socket is a production incident waiting for enough traffic** — and the two look identical at the call site, which is why the question has to be asked of the body rather than the signature.

d.title: Three entry points, and only one belongs in a server
d.caption: **`run` manages its own event loop, so calling it from inside a coroutine either raises or deadlocks depending on how your framework set things up.** In a FastAPI handler, an ADK plugin or any async context, `run_async` is the only correct choice — `run` exists so a notebook cell does not need `asyncio.run`, and that is the whole of its purpose. **`run_live` is a different protocol with a different model requirement**, not a streaming flag on the same path.

d.title: One in-flight turn per session id - and ADK does not enforce it
d.caption: **Two turns of the same session read the same state and append to the same event list, so interleaving them produces a transcript where the deltas were applied in an order nobody intended.** Nothing stops two HTTP handlers calling `run_async` with the same session id at once. **Most interfaces get the rule for free** because a user cannot send a second message mid-stream — but an API client, a retry, an impatient double-click or a reconnecting websocket each break it. A lock keyed by session id is a small amount of code against a confusing class of corruption.

d.title: Three modes, and what the default already gives you
d.caption: **Events already stream in every mode**, because `run_async` is an async generator: a tool call appears the moment the model asks for it and the result appears the moment the tool returns. That alone is enough to show “checking stock…” while work happens. **So `StreamingMode.SSE` adds exactly one thing — the model's text arriving in pieces** — and BIDI is not more of the same but a different protocol with a different model requirement.

d.title: Append the deltas, replace on the final - or the answer appears twice
d.caption: **The final event carries the whole answer, not the last fragment**, so a client that treats it as another delta renders the reply twice — and that is exactly what the naive loop produces. Branch on `event.partial` and the bug cannot happen. **And do the first branch before anything clever with text:** the biggest perceived-latency win in an agent is usually not token streaming but telling the user that something is happening, and “searching the policy documents…” comes from an event you already receive.

d.title: The thing between you and the browser that buffers the whole stream
d.caption: **A reverse proxy with response buffering on, a compression layer, or a serverless platform that waits for the complete body will collect your stream and deliver it in one piece** — and the agent looks exactly as slow as it did before you implemented streaming, with no error anywhere to explain it. **So test through the real deployment path rather than against the local server**, and check for `X-Accel-Buffering` or the equivalent in whatever sits in front. Note also that streaming changes nothing about identity: the user id is still derived server-side.

nodes.label: The browser gets it all at once
nodes.sub: as slow as before, and no error

d.title: By default the exception comes out of run_async, and the turn ends
d.caption: **Your HTTP handler sees it, the user sees whatever your error page says, and the conversation is left with an incomplete event log.** For a genuine bug that is exactly right — you want it in the error tracker rather than swallowed. **For an upstream that is briefly unavailable it is a poor outcome**, because the agent could simply have said so and carried on. The whole of this lesson is deciding which failures are which.

nodes.label: For a real bug: correct
nodes.sub: you want it in the tracker

nodes.label: For a flaky upstream: poor

d.title: Three details to copy, and the one line never to write
d.caption: **`return {"error": str(error)}` is the reflex, and it hands the model — and therefore the user, and therefore anyone who asks — your hostnames, table names, file paths and occasionally a connection string.** Log the real exception with the invocation id so you can find it, and give the model a description in terms the user could hear. **The `retryable` key is the third detail:** it tells the model whether trying again is sensible, which an unadorned message does not.

d.title: Five runaways, and the bound for each - starting with the one you already have
d.caption: **`max_llm_calls` defaults to 500, which is a backstop rather than a budget:** it exists so a pathological loop terminates eventually, and by the time you reach it you have spent a great deal of money on one question. Set it to a plausible turn for your agent — a support agent that has made thirty model calls is not working, it is stuck. **And note the last row:** the framework's bounds do not cover a slow upstream holding the turn open. That needs a timeout in the tool's own HTTP client.

d.title: Four things a good failure message does
d.caption: **The second row is why converting errors into results is a correctness issue and not only a UX one:** if a refund tool failed, the answer must not say the refund was issued. **And the fourth is the cheapest support investment in the whole course** — the invocation id in the message turns “it didn't work yesterday” from an unreproducible complaint into a log lookup. Keeping the conversation alive matters too: a failure that ends the session throws away context the user then has to re-establish.
